c.tagline: Windswept Atlantic medina of blue boats, ramparts, and Gnaoua rhythm.

taxi.fareNote: Small blue 'petits taxis' handle trips inside town — metered by law but many run short flat fares (around 10-20 DH); larger cream 'grands taxis' cover the airport and out-of-town runs. No Uber or Bolt operate in Essaouira.

emergency.note: 19 reaches the police in towns and cities; 15 is the ambulance/medical emergency line (177 for the Gendarmerie Royale on rural roads).

hood_landmark.Kasbah: Skala de la Ville Essaouira clock tower

avoid.reason: Politely brush off faux guides and touts around the medina and port, watch pockets in crowded souks, and skip unlit medina alleys late at night.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed walled old town, a compact grid of whitewashed, blue-shuttered lanes packed with souks, artisan workshops, riads, and the fish-grilling port at its edge; the obvious first-timer base, everything on foot.
The oldest fortified quarter of the medina by the Skala ramparts and the clock tower, lined with galleries, cafes, and the town's grandest riads; central and atmospheric.

A quieter, more residential pocket of the eastern medina near Bab Doukkala, with local bakeries, small guesthouses, and everyday markets rather than tourist souks; a calmer, authentic base still inside the walls.

The newer district stretching south along the Atlantic beachfront below the medina, home to seafront hotels, surf and kitesurf schools, and wide open sand; best for water-sports travelers wanting room and sea breeze.

A small village across the Oued Ksob about 10 minutes south, backed by dunes and the ruined Borj el Berod fort, with the Sofitel golf resort and a laid-back rural feel; suits those wanting quiet, riding, and golf away from the crowds.
lodging: Le Médina Essaouira Thalassa Sea & Spa - MGallery

water.note: Tap is treated but most visitors drink bottled water.

transit.hours: Petits taxis run through the day and evening; the medina is walkable at all hours.
transit.note: Essaouira is small and almost entirely walkable within the walled medina; there is no urban bus network, so short hops rely on blue petits taxis.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash (dirhams); confirm the fare or that the meter is running before setting off.

Local grands taxis to nearby towns
train: No rail service — nearest station is Marrakech (~3 hr by coach)

transit.m: Grand taxi (shared/cream) to the medina (~15 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants; round up for cafes and taxis. A few dirhams for porters and parking wardens is the norm.

food.name: Charcoal-Grilled Sardines
food.desc: Atlantic sardines landed that morning, salted and grilled whole over coals at the port stalls, eaten with bread, tomato salad and lemon.

places.name: Ocean Vagabond

food.name: Fish Tagine with Chermoula

places.name: Restaurant Blue Mogador

places.name: Restaurant Ferdaous

places.name: La Table by Madada

places.name: Elizir
places.note: Vintage-furnished favourite blending Moroccan and Italian; book ahead, it is small.

places.name: Restaurant Blue Mogador
places.note: Reliable, affordable pastilla in both seafood and chicken versions.

places.name: Souk Jdid stalls

places.name: Triskala Cafe
places.note: Serves homemade Moroccan breads and pancakes with argan oil and honey.

food.desc: Steamed semolina piled with seven vegetables and lamb or fish, ladled with broth; traditionally eaten after Friday prayers.

places.name: Restaurant Ferdaous

places.name: La Table by Madada

food.desc: Green gunpowder tea steeped with fresh spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from height to build a foam; served all day, everywhere.

places.name: Chez Driss

places.name: Skala de la Ville cafes

landmarks: Medina of Essaouira
A UNESCO-listed 18th-century walled town of whitewashed lanes and blue shutters, designed by a European architect for a Moroccan sultan.
Skala de la Ville
The Atlantic-battered sea bastion crowned with brass cannons, a Game of Thrones filming spot with wave-crashed ramparts made for sunset.
Skala du Port and the Fishing Harbor
The photogenic fortified port where cobalt-blue wooden boats unload sardines beneath screaming gulls and the crenellated harbor gate.
Place Moulay Hassan
The medina's cafe-fringed main square, where gnawa musicians, orange-juice carts and grilled-sardine stalls animate the space between port and souks.
Essaouira Beach
A vast crescent of sand pounded by reliable trade winds, making the bay one of Africa's premier windsurfing and kitesurfing arenas.
Mogador Island (Iles Purpuraires)
The offshore archipelago that sheltered Phoenician purple-dye works and now guards Eleonora's falcons, framing every sunset photo from the ramparts.
Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdallah Museum
A former pasha's riad displaying carpets, jewelry, woodwork and musical instruments that trace Essaouira's Amazigh, Arab and Jewish heritage.
Mellah and Haim Pinto Synagogue
The old Jewish quarter, once home to nearly half the city, where the restored blue-and-white synagogue of Rabbi Haim Pinto still draws pilgrims.
The Souks and Fish Market
The medina's thuya-wood carvers, spice pyramids and argan-oil cooperatives cluster along Avenue de l'Istiqlal around the raucous fish auction.
Diabat and the Borj El Berod ruins
A half-buried beach fortress crumbling into the dunes near the village Jimi Hendrix made famous, reached by a camel-friendly shoreline walk.

train.note: No passenger rail reaches Essaouira. Supratours runs a coach connection timed to meet ONCF trains (https://www.oncf-voyages.ma/) at Marrakech station, sold as a single through ticket, which is the usual way in from Casablanca or Tangier. There is also a small airport with seasonal European flights.

bus.note: No international coaches. CTM (https://www.ctm.ma/) and Supratours (https://www.supratours.ma/) run frequent coaches to Marrakech in about 3 hours, Agadir in 3 and Casablanca in 6, from the Bab Marrakech gare routière just outside the medina walls. Supratours is the one to book if you want the rail connection at Marrakech.

ferry.note: Essaouira's harbour is a working fishing port with no scheduled passenger service - the blue boats you see are trawlers. Short trips out to the Îles Purpuraires are seasonal and restricted, since the islands are a falcon reserve.

full.blurb: The imperial 'Red City' of Jemaa el-Fnaa, souks and palaces, about 3 hours inland by coach.
